content: 1. Positive needs and data validation are essential components of the process. 2. Checklist 7 involves a comprehensive review of outpatient staff capacities. 3. In Section 2, facility staff utilize data to identify and prioritize actions for a three-month action plan. 4. Section 3 focuses on synthesizing findings from reviews conducted across multiple facilities, using Checklists 1–7 and synthesis tables to consolidate results. 5. Section 4 emphasizes completing monitoring and evaluation tables (Tables 4–8) specifically for family planning services. 6. Section 5 outlines the development of an annual implementation plan, linking it to previous plans and completing an action framework. 7. Facilitators must obtain clearance from local health officers and subnational authorities to visit selected facilities. A letter of introduction from the Ministry of Health is often required for courtesy calls with facility chiefs or their designates. 8. Health facility staff (one or two individuals) should be identified and supported to organize reviews, learn the approach, and coordinate the implementation of the facility plan, with agreement from senior staff. 9. Budgeting is necessary to cover per diem for facilitators, transportation, photocopying, and other associated costs. 10. A designated room within the facility should be identified for staff training, record review, data synthesis, and planning activities. 11. Periodic evaluations at district, subnational, or national levels require at least 12 evaluators for an assessment of 18 hospitals. These evaluators may include members of family planning departments, facility teams, Ministry of Health staff, and development partners. 12. The evaluation process typically spans six to eight days, including preparation, fieldwork, and data analysis for annual planning. 13. Site selection for assessments can follow two options: Option 1: Include all health facilities that initiated monitoring within the past year. Option 2: Randomly select at least 18 facilities for national or subnational reviews, ensuring representation across different levels (national, regional, provincial, district, and subdistrict). 14. Public facilities are usually the focus of assessments, but private providers may also be included if they deliver a significant proportion of care. Sampling should reflect the proportion of care provided by public and private sectors. 15. Evaluators should conduct two days of training and plan field logistics, ensuring the availability of meeting venues, supplies, and necessary documents. 16. Monitoring and evaluation tables should be completed in advance, except for sections requiring facility-specific data. 17. Interviews with clients and chart reviews are conducted to assess the effectiveness of family planning services. 18. Evaluators should arrive at facilities before clinic sessions begin and identify outpatient clinics serving women aged 15–49 years. 19. Client registers are used to select eligible women for interviews, ensuring a representative sample size. 20. Verbal informed consent must be obtained from participants, emphasizing confidentiality and voluntary participation. 21. Interviews should be conducted in a private setting, such as a designated room or quiet area, to ensure privacy. 22. Questions during interviews focus on the day of the visit, and responses are recorded systematically using standardized codes (e.g., Y for Yes, N for No). 23. Client records are reviewed alongside interview responses to gather comprehensive data. 24. Women are screened for eligibility based on their reproductive intentions, such as delaying or avoiding childbearing. 25. Health workers should ensure selected women remain in the waiting area after their clinic visit for interviews. 26. Questions address current contraceptive use, primary methods, and any issues or concerns with these methods. 27. Health workers should discuss the risks, side effects, and effectiveness of contraceptive methods with clients, addressing their fears and concerns. 28. Clients should be informed about the availability and advantages of long-acting reversible contraceptive methods, such as IUDs and implants. 29. Accessibility and cost of contraceptive methods, including travel time and affordability, should be assessed to understand their impact on clients' decisions. 30. Clients should be asked about their knowledge of where to access permanent methods (e.g., tubal ligation, vasectomy) and termination of pregnancy services. 31. If clients have experienced barriers to obtaining an abortion, reasons should be documented, such as lack of knowledge, fear of complications, or social restrictions. 32. The evaluation process aims to improve counseling and contraceptive usage by addressing gaps in service delivery and client education.
